oneSentence: A small, carefully chosen change to an input can push a model towards a wrong output while looking almost unchanged to a person.
plainExplanation:
An adversarial example is an input that has been intentionally altered so a machine-learning model gives the wrong result. The change may be tiny: a few pixels in an image, a few words in a prompt, or a small pattern in audio. To a person, the input may look normal or nearly normal.

What goes in is usually a normal input plus a targeted modification. What happens is that the modification exploits the model’s sensitivity to particular patterns in its data representation. A representation is the internal numerical form the model uses. The model then produces an output that is wrong, misleading, or chosen by the attacker.

What comes out depends on the system. In image classification, a stop sign might be labelled incorrectly. In speech recognition, background noise might shift a transcription. In language models, the closest equivalent is often not a tiny pixel-like change but a crafted string of text that steers behaviour. That is why this term overlaps with, but is not the same as, prompt injection or jailbreak.

The term is often confused with adversarial attack. An adversarial example is the manipulated input itself. An adversarial attack is the broader method or campaign used to create or deliver such inputs. It is also different from poor general performance: a model can seem accurate on normal tests but still fail badly on specially designed inputs.

everydayAnalogy.title: A shipping label altered by one subtle mark
everydayAnalogy.story: At a port warehouse, a worker checks whether a shipping manifest matches the delivery. Most labels are easy to read, but one crate has a small extra pen mark placed next to a printed code. To the worker, it still looks like the same destination code at a glance, yet the scanning system reads it as a different warehouse and routes the crate incorrectly. The crate, the goods and most of the label stay the same; the mistake comes from a tiny change positioned to exploit how the scanner reads characters.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A scanner usually follows fixed character-reading rules, while many AI models respond to complex numerical patterns learned from data. In real adversarial examples, the change is often optimised mathematically, not added by eye. Also, some attacks on language models rely on meaningful text instructions, not subtle marks that humans would miss.

visual.title: Normal input and adversarial input through the same model
visual.learningObjective: Show how a very small, intentional input change can produce a very different model output without changing the model itself.
visual.description: A two-column diagram compares the same model receiving two nearly identical inputs. Read left to right: original input to model to expected output, then slightly altered input to the same model to wrong output. A highlight overlay marks the tiny changed region or token.

steps.label: Original input
steps.explanation: Show a normal input, such as an image of a road sign or a short text prompt, with no highlighted changes.
steps.visualInstruction: Render a card on the left labelled 'original input'. Include a simple image or text block. Use neutral colours and no warning icons.

steps.label: Same model
steps.explanation: The model itself does not change between the two cases.
steps.visualInstruction: Place one central model box used by both paths, or two identical model boxes with the same label and styling: 'same trained model'.

steps.label: Expected output
steps.explanation: With the original input, the model gives the correct or expected result.
steps.visualInstruction: Connect the original input to the model and then to a green output card labelled with a correct classification or safe behaviour.

steps.label: Tiny intentional change
steps.explanation: A small, targeted alteration is added to the input. It may be visually minor but strategically chosen.
steps.visualInstruction: Show a second input card below or to the right of the first. Highlight only the changed pixels, patch, or inserted text span with a thin outline or accent colour.

steps.label: Wrong output
steps.explanation: The altered input passes through the same model but now triggers a wrong result.
steps.visualInstruction: Connect the altered input to the identical model and then to a red or amber output card labelled with the incorrect prediction or steered response.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap the changed region to toggle a magnified inset and a short note saying 'small change to input, large change to output'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two cases using the same trained model. In the first case, an original input goes into the model and produces the expected output. In the second case, a nearly identical input with one small highlighted change goes into the same model and produces a wrong output. The point is that the model need not be altered or hacked internally; changing the input alone can be enough to change the result.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side comparison replaces any hover or animation. The changed part of the second input remains outlined, and both input-to-output paths are visible at once.

workedExample.scenario: An image classifier used in a warehouse sorts parcels by hazard label.
workedExample.input: Original image: a parcel with a clearly visible 'flammable' diamond. Altered image: the same parcel photo with a faint printed sticker pattern added over one corner.
process: The original photo is sent to the classifier, which outputs 'flammable' with 0.94 confidence.
An attacker tests small overlay patterns and finds one that changes the model’s internal representation.
The altered photo looks almost the same to staff viewing a thumbnail.
The same classifier processes the altered photo and outputs 'general goods' with 0.71 confidence.
workedExample.result: A tiny, deliberate visual change to the input causes a materially different label, even though the object in the scene has not changed.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN team uses an approved internal tool to help triage incoming public social media images for a situation report, separating damaged infrastructure photos from unrelated content.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: If someone deliberately edits images or text snippets to fool the model, the triage queue may misclassify important material or elevate misleading content. Staff need to recognise that model error can be induced, not only accidental.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential, personal, protection-sensitive or security-sensitive material to an unapproved public AI service for testing. Any review of suspected adversarial inputs should stay within approved systems and human oversight.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, this matters because a system that performs well in routine testing may still be fragile in practice. If a model can be pushed off course by small, crafted changes, then safety, quality control, procurement and risk assessments need to ask different questions: not only 'How accurate is it on average?' but also 'How does it fail under manipulation?' This affects decisions about whether a model can be trusted for screening, routing, monitoring or support tasks, what human review is needed, and what safeguards such as input filtering, rate limits, sandboxing and fallback procedures should be in place.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An adversarial example means the system was hacked in the usual network-security sense.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. The attacker may never break into the server or steal credentials. They may only supply a specially crafted input that the model processes exactly as designed, but in a way that exposes a weakness in the model’s learned patterns.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If humans can still read or see the input, the model should also handle it.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Humans and models rely on different cues. A small change that seems irrelevant to a person can shift the numerical features the model uses a great deal. That mismatch is why human inspection alone does not guarantee model robustness.

Images are the classic example, but the idea extends to audio, text and other data types. In language models, however, many practical attacks are better described as prompt injection or jailbreaks, because they use meaningful instructions rather than imperceptible perturbations.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A model can be tricked by an input that looks almost normal to a person but has been altered on purpose to cause a wrong answer.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: An adversarial example is a test-time input modified by an adversary to induce model error or a target output. The perturbation may be constrained to remain small under some distance measure or perceptual bound, but it is optimised to move the input across a decision boundary or otherwise change the model’s output distribution. In practice, attacks may be white-box, using gradients or other model knowledge, or black-box, using queries and transferability. The exact mechanism differs by modality: in vision, it often involves pixel-space or patch perturbations; in speech, waveform changes; in text, token substitutions, insertions or control strings, though for language models many real incidents are more precisely classified under prompt injection or jailbreak. The key distinction is between the crafted input instance and the broader adversarial attack process used to generate or deploy it.

keyTakeaway: A tiny, deliberate change to the input can be enough to make a model fail, even when nothing visible about the real-world situation has changed.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best distinguishes an adversarial example from an adversarial attack?
options: An adversarial example is the crafted input; an adversarial attack is the broader method used to create or deliver it.
An adversarial example only applies to images, while an adversarial attack only applies to language models.
An adversarial example changes the model weights directly, while an adversarial attack changes only the user interface.
They are identical terms and can always be used interchangeably.
quickCheck.explanation: The example is the manipulated input instance itself. The attack is the wider process, strategy or technique that creates, selects or sends that input. People often use the terms loosely, but the distinction matters when analysing defences and incidents.

issues.problem: The text examples blur adversarial examples into prompt injection and jailbreak. Saying that a crafted string which “steers behaviour” is the closest language-model equivalent does not identify what makes it an adversarial example. Meaningful instructions intended to override rules fit the separate prompt injection or jailbreak entries. Text adversarial examples can instead involve crafted token changes intended to alter a prediction or output without functioning as instructions.
issues.fix: Replace the explanation with the corrected version below, which distinguishes crafted text perturbations from instruction-based attacks.

issues.problem: The claim that a scanner “usually follows fixed character-reading rules” is unreliable. Character recognition systems can themselves use models and learned numerical patterns. The distinction therefore does not state a valid general limitation of the analogy.
issues.fix: The scanner handles a narrow code format, while AI models may respond to complex numerical patterns learned from data. Real adversarial changes are often optimised mathematically, not added by eye. Some attacks on language models use meaningful instructions and are better classified as prompt injection or jailbreak.

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer. Option 1 is false because both concepts can apply across modalities. Option 2 is false because neither term is distinguished by changing weights or the user interface. Option 3 contradicts the distinction stated throughout the page. However, all three distractors are so plainly absurd that the answer can be selected without understanding the term.
issues.fix: Keep option 0. Replace the distractors with: “An adversarial example is the wrong output; an adversarial attack is the input that caused it.”; “An adversarial example is one crafted input; an adversarial attack is any failure on unusual data.”; “An adversarial example needs model internals; an adversarial attack can use external queries.”
